W1. Linear Programming Basics

Author

Mohammad Reza Bahrami

Published

September 10, 2026

1. Theory

1.1 Foundations and Core Philosophy of Optimization

Optimization is the purposeful discipline and mathematical process of finding the best possible decision—maximizing or minimizing a given quantitative criterion—among a collection of available alternatives, subject to prescribed conditions or restrictions. Formally, an optimization problem seeks an optimal parameter vector within a defined search domain such that:

where is the objective function (or cost function), and the feasible domain is delineated by functional constraints and parameter boundaries. The fundamental purpose across science, engineering, operations research, and economics extends far beyond finding a merely valid or feasible solution (any point satisfying the constraints); human intention aims to determine the optimal solution that achieves the absolute extreme of the objective criterion.

  • Why It Matters: Real-world systems—whether allocating production resources, training machine learning models, or routing transport networks—possess scarce resources and competing operational choices. Optimization converts qualitative decision-making into rigorous mathematical formulations, deriving formal criteria for the existence, uniqueness, and computability of peak system performance.
  • The Algorithmic Imperative (Exact vs. Iterative Solvers): A central peculiarity of operations research is that practical models rarely yield closed-form algebraic solutions (explicit “plug-in” formulas). Instead, solutions must be generated by numerical algorithms—prescribed sequences of computational operations executed iteratively: where each iteration attempts to transition the candidate vector closer to the true optimum . Because repetitive algebraic computations over multiple dimensions are tedious and voluminous, modern optimization is inherently computer-assisted. This reliance on iterative algorithms introduces four core computational challenges:
    1. Convergence speed: The rate at which the error sequence approaches zero (e.g., linear, superlinear, or quadratic convergence).
    2. Numerical precision and error tolerance: Floating-point rounding limits, machine precision, and stopping thresholds .
    3. Computational complexity: The scaling of iteration runtimes and memory demands as the number of variables and constraints expands.
    4. Algorithmic trapping: Distinguishing between local optima and global extrema depending on model convexity.
  • Heuristic Search Fallback: When mathematical formulations exhibit extreme combinatorial explosion, non-smoothness, or NP-hard computational barriers, finding a provably exact optimum within a feasible timeframe becomes impossible. Under these circumstances, exact algorithms are abandoned in favor of heuristics—intelligent, rule-of-thumb search procedures (such as greedy priority rules, local neighborhood searches, simulated annealing, or genetic algorithms). Heuristics sacrifice theoretical guarantees of absolute optimality to locate acceptable, high-quality, near-optimal solutions within practical computational budgets.
  • Worked Mini-Illustration: Consider choosing an operating parameter to minimize the quadratic operating loss .
    • Closed-form approach: Setting the derivative yields the exact stationary minimum with directly.
    • Iterative gradient step approach: If represents a black-box response evaluated via an iterative update with step size starting from an initial guess :
      • Iteration 1: , reducing loss from to .
      • Iteration 2: , further reducing loss to . Successive algorithmic evaluations generate a sequence converging toward .
  • Key Pitfalls: Confusing feasibility with optimality. A solution is feasible if it merely obeys every system constraint; it is optimal only if no other feasible vector yields a superior objective value. Conversely, assuming that every optimization problem admits a closed-form formula overlooks the inherently algorithmic, iterative nature of computational solvers and the necessity of heuristic approximations when scaling limits are reached.
1.2 Data-Driven Optimization Motivating Examples

A data-driven optimization problem is a mathematical formulation where the objective function, constraints, or both are constructed directly from empirical observations, measurements, or network topologies rather than purely theoretical laws. In modern computing, optimization serves as the computational engine for extracting structure, learning representations, and finding optimal discrete configurations from data.

Why this matters: across scientific computing, artificial intelligence, and operations research, practical problems rarely arrive as pre-packaged equations. Framing raw data as an optimization problem bridges real-world measurements and rigorous algorithmic solutions.

Three fundamental paradigms demonstrate how diverse data models translate into concrete optimization problems:

1.2.1 Least-Squares Linear Regression as Continuous Unconstrained Optimization

When fitting an affine-linear model to experimental observations , the goal is to find parameters that best explain the data. For an overdetermined system where (more data points than model parameters), no straight line passes through all points simultaneously, making the linear system inconsistent.

The task is formulated as minimizing the squared Euclidean norm of the residual error vector :

Geometrically, this is an orthogonal projection of the measurement vector onto the column space of , denoted . The error vector must be orthogonal to every column of , leading directly to the normal equations:

  • Worked Illustration: Consider three experimental measurements: at , at , and at . If the line passed through all three points, it would satisfy: Because these three points are not collinear, has no exact solution. Formulating the normal equations: Solving the system: The unique least-squares optimal affine model is . Evaluating this fitted line at the sample times produces the projection vector , which minimizes the total sum of squared residuals .
1.2.2 Training Artificial Neural Networks as Parameter Misfit Minimization

In supervised machine learning, an artificial neural network models an unknown target relationship using a parameterized network architecture. Given a training dataset with feature vectors and corresponding target labels , a single artificial neuron computes a linear combination of its inputs shifted by a scalar bias , which is then passed through an activation function : where denotes the synaptic weights.

Training the neuron corresponds to an unconstrained continuous optimization problem: adjust decision vector to minimize a scalar misfit objective function over all training samples: where is a loss metric (such as squared error ). In realistic multi-layer perceptrons, this principle extends directly: the model becomes a deep concatenation of alternating linear transfers and nonlinear activations, resulting in a highly non-convex, high-dimensional parameter optimization problem solved via iterative gradient algorithms.

1.2.3 Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP) as Combinatorial Graph Optimization

Unlike regression and neural network training where decision variables live in continuous spaces (), network routing problems operate on discrete combinatorial structures.

In the Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP), given a set of vertices (cities) connected by edges with associated non-negative weights (such as flight airfares, distances, or transit times), the goal is to find a closed tour (Hamiltonian cycle) that visits every city exactly once and returns to the departure city with the minimum total cost: subject to:

  • Each city is entered exactly once.
  • Each city is exited exactly once.
  • Subtours (disconnected sub-cycles that do not span all vertices) are strictly eliminated.
  • Conceptual Example (Airfare Routing): Given a complete network of five cities—San Francisco, Los Angeles, Denver, Detroit, New York—with known pairwise non-directional airfares (e.g., San Francisco–Los Angeles: , San Francisco–Denver: , San Francisco–Detroit: , Detroit–New York: , etc.), solving the TSP requires searching the discrete permutations of vertices to select the cycle minimizing total ticket price.
1.2.4 Pitfalls and Typical Confusions
  • Exact Solvability vs. Best Approximation: A frequent mistake when handling inconsistent systems is attempting to find a vector satisfying . In overdetermined data problems, an exact solution does not exist; optimization defines what “best” means (e.g., minimizing squared Euclidean error via ) rather than solving an exact linear system.
  • Continuous vs. Combinatorial Complexity: In continuous unconstrained convex problems like least squares, the global optimum can often be expressed analytically via normal equations or reached reliably via gradients. In discrete combinatorial problems like TSP, the solution space grows factorially ( undirected tours for cities), rendering brute-force enumeration impossible for large instances and necessitating specialized integer programming formulations or heuristics.
1.3 Problem Anatomy, Decision Frameworks, and Operations Research Phases

Every mathematical optimization model rests on three foundational pillars: 1. Decision alternatives (or decision variables): Controllable quantities whose values the decision-maker selects. 2. Constraints: Restrictions, physical limits, or operational demands that dictate which values of are permissible, expressed as inequalities () and equalities (). 3. Objective criterion (or objective function): An evaluative metric that maps candidate decisions to a scalar value to be minimized or maximized.

A candidate decision is a feasible solution if it satisfies every constraint simultaneously: for all , for all , and . The collection of all such points forms the feasible set (or feasible solution space), denoted by . A model is infeasible if its feasible set is empty (). A solution is an optimal solution if for all in a minimization problem (or in a maximization problem). A mathematical program is called solvable if it admits at least one optimal solution.

1.3.1 Operations Research Method Taxonomy

Operations Research (OR) does not rely on a single monolithic algorithm. Methods are classified into four broad methodological branches:

  • Mathematical programming: Techniques to optimize a function subject to deterministic constraints. Subdivided by structure into calculus and variational methods, linear programming (LP), integer programming (IP), dynamic programming (DP), nonlinear programming (NLP), quadratic programming (QP), network methods, and game theory.
  • Stochastic process techniques: Methods for analyzing systems governed by probabilistic mechanisms and random variables, including Markov processes, queueing theory, renewal theory, reliability theory, and simulation models.
  • Statistical methods: Empirical modeling and inference strategies, including linear and nonlinear regression, cluster analysis, discriminant analysis, and design of experiments (DoE).
  • Modern or nontraditional optimization techniques: Metaheuristics and nature-inspired algorithms developed for complex, non-convex, or NP-hard landscapes where exact algorithms stall, including genetic algorithms (GA), simulated annealing (SA), particle swarm optimization (PSO), ant colony optimization (ACO), neural networks, and fuzzy optimization.
1.3.2 The Five Phases of an Operations Research Study

Translating a real-world dilemma into operational practice follows five sequential phases: 1. Problem definition: Identifying the system boundaries, relevant stakeholders, resource limits, decision alternatives, and the primary objective criterion. 2. Model construction: Translating verbal descriptions and empirical measurements into mathematical functions, equations, and sets (, , ). 3. Model solution: Applying exact mathematical programming algorithms or heuristics to compute optimal or near-optimal decisions . This third phase is the best-defined and mathematically most tractable phase of an OR project, as it operates on formal, self-contained equations. 4. Model validation: Testing whether the mathematical abstraction represents the real system with sufficient fidelity (e.g., verifying against historical data and stress-testing edge cases). 5. Implementation: Translating algorithmic outputs into standard operating procedures, software workflows, and operational decision rules. Phases 1, 2, 4, and 5 represent an interactive human art rather than pure closed-form theory.

1.3.3 Worked Illustration: Multi-Week Ticket Purchasing Problem

A businessperson has a 5-week recurring commitment requiring travel from Kazan (KZN) to Moscow (MOS), departing KZN every Monday morning and returning from MOS every Wednesday afternoon. The airline pricing schedule is:

  • Regular roundtrip ticket: .
  • Weekend-spanning roundtrip ticket: discount .
  • One-way ticket (either direction): of regular roundtrip price .

Decision Problem Formulation:

  • Alternatives: Discrete ticket-purchasing schedules spanning the 5-week horizon.
  • Constraint: The traveler must depart KZN on Monday and return on Wednesday of the exact same week for each of the 5 consecutive weeks.
  • Objective criterion: Minimize total purchasing expenditure.

Evaluation of Discrete Strategies:

  • Alternative 1 (Independent weekly tickets): Purchase 5 standard same-week roundtrips (KZN–MOS–KZN). None span a weekend.
  • Alternative 2 (One-way boundaries + reverse weekend roundtrips): Purchase one one-way KZN MOS on Monday of Week 1, four weekend-spanning roundtrips originating in Moscow (MOS–KZN–MOS) covering Wednesdays of Week to Mondays of Week (), and one final one-way MOS KZN on Wednesday of Week 5:
  • Alternative 3 (Staggered weekend-spanning tickets): Purchase one KZN–MOS–KZN roundtrip ticket departing Monday of Week 1 and returning Wednesday of Week 5 (spanning 4 weekends; cost ). Cover the intermediate trips using four nested MOS–KZN–MOS roundtrip tickets departing Wednesday of Week and returning Monday of Week for (each spanning one weekend; cost each). All 5 purchased tickets span at least one weekend:

Every alternative satisfies the operational calendar restriction (), making all three feasible. Because , Alternative 3 is the unique optimal solution, achieving an expenditure of .

1.3.4 Pitfalls and Conceptual Distinctions
  • Closed-Form Formulas vs. Iterative Algorithms: Unlike elementary calculus problems where unconstrained optima are computed by setting derivatives directly to zero () and solving algebraically, OR models generally lack closed-form solutions. They require iterative algorithms that systematically generate a sequence of points moving monotonically toward the optimum.
  • Model Infeasibility vs. Algorithm Failure: An empty feasible set () is an intrinsic structural property of mutually contradictory constraints (e.g., and ), not a failure of the numerical solver. If a problem is infeasible, no optimal solution exists.
  • Mathematical Optimality vs. Practical Fidelity: An algorithmically optimal solution optimizes only the specific mathematical formulation provided. If Phase 1 (definition) or Phase 2 (construction) omits latent real-world constraints, may prove practically unworkable or sub-optimal in Phase 5.
1.4 Mathematical Programming Formulations and Problem Taxonomies

A general constrained mathematical programming problem is defined as finding a decision vector that minimizes an objective function (or cost function) over a prescribed feasible domain: where are inequality constraints, are equality constraints, and denotes the underlying ground set. The number of variables and the constraint counts and are independent. When and , the problem becomes an unconstrained optimization problem:

Problems are categorized primarily by their decision domain :

  • Continuous Optimization: The domain is a continuum, such as the full space , a box domain , or a unit simplex . The functions are typically continuous or differentiable over .
  • Discrete (Combinatorial) Optimization: The domain consists of discrete, isolated points, such as the integer lattice or binary vectors .

Within continuous optimization, structure dictates solvability:

  • Linear Optimization (LO / LP): The domain is , and all functions , , and are strictly affine (linear combinations of variables plus a constant).
  • Convex Optimization: The ground set is convex, each equality constraint is affine, and the objective as well as all inequality constraints are convex functions, satisfying the Jensen-type inequality:
  • Nonlinear Continuous Optimization: At least one of the objective or constraint functions contains nonlinear terms that fail convexity or affine requirements.
1.4.1 The Representation Criterion

Optimization taxonomy adheres to the representation criterion: a problem’s class is strictly determined by how its mathematical model is explicitly formulated, not by any equivalent problem into which it could hypothetically be transformed.

  • Nonlinear vs. Linear Representation: Although the constraint system is purely linear and is strictly monotonic (meaning minimizing yields the exact same minimizer as minimizing ), this model is not a linear program. The objective expression is nonlinear; hence, as presented, it belongs to nonlinear continuous optimization.
  • Finite vs. Semi-Infinite Representation: Even though every single constraint is affine, the index set generates an infinite family of constraints. A standard linear programming model requires a finite constraint index (). Consequently, this formulation is classified as a semi-infinite programming problem rather than a standard linear program.
1.4.2 Why Problem Taxonomy Matters

Algorithm design depends entirely on taxonomy: linear programs admit finite polynomial-time interior point methods and vertex-hopping simplex pivots; convex problems guarantee that any local minimum is a global minimum; and discrete combinatorial problems often require branch-and-bound or cutting-plane routines due to NP-hardness. Misclassifying an analytical model risks deploying algorithms whose convergence guarantees do not apply.

1.4.3 Worked Illustration

Consider classifying the following two formulations:

  1. Formulation A: Classification: is convex (), and is affine (thus convex). The domain is (continuous). This is a linearly constrained convex quadratic program (a subfield of continuous convex optimization).
  2. Formulation B: Classification: The objective and constraint functions are linear, but the variable domain is . Because the domain is non-continuous, it is classified as a binary integer linear program (combinatorial optimization), not a continuous linear program.
1.4.4 Common Pitfalls
  • Confusing Equivalent Solutions with Equivalent Problem Classes: Transforming an objective via a monotonic transformation (e.g., replacing with ) produces identical optimal points , but the first is non-differentiable at zero while the second is a smooth quadratic program. Taxonomy applies strictly to the written algebraic form.
  • Assuming Linear Constraints Imply a Linear Program: A problem where all constraints are linear hyperplanes is still classified as nonlinear if the objective contains powers, products of variables, or transcendental functions.
  • Overlooking Constraint Cardinality: Linearity of every individual constraint function is insufficient if the constraint index set is unbounded; infinite sets of linear inequalities define semi-infinite programs, which require specialized functional-analytic solution methods.
1.5 Linear Programming Modeling and Canonical Equivalence Transformations

A linear programming (LP) problem (or linear optimization problem) is a mathematical program whose objective function and all functional constraints are affine (linear) expressions of continuous decision variables over a finite constraint index set:

Linearly constrained problems with nonlinear terms (such as or ) or with an infinite collection of constraints (such as for all integers ) violate this definition and cannot be processed by standard linear programming algorithms. Furthermore, an optimization problem is categorized as an LP strictly based on its explicit formulation, not on whether a nonlinear presentation might be indirectly transformed into one.

1.5.1 Why Canonical Form Matters

Theoretical algorithms (such as the simplex tableau, interior-point methods, and duality theory) assume a single, standardized mathematical structure. Expressing every problem in a unified format—the canonical maximization form—eliminates edge cases in algorithm design, proves general duality theorems, and enables general-purpose matrix solvers.

1.5.2 Canonical Representation Formats

In canonical form, the goal is always maximization, and all functional constraints are expressed as “” inequalities: 1. Term-Wise Notation: 2. Constraint-Wise Notation: where and each . 3. Matrix-Vector Notation: where has rows , and .

1.5.3 Algebraic Equivalence Rules

Any general linear program maps into canonical form via four fundamental algebraic operations: 1. Reversing Inequality Direction: An inequality of type is multiplied by to reverse its relation: 2. Splitting Equalities into Opposing Inequalities: An equality constraint holds if and only if both and hold simultaneously. Negating the second relation yields two canonical inequalities: 3. Objective Inversion: Minimizing a linear function over a feasible set is mathematically equivalent to maximizing its negative, : 4. Handling Non-negativity Constraints: Non-negativity constraints are functional inequalities rewritten as to fit the matrix constraint system .

1.5.6 Pitfalls and Modeling Traps
  • Ratio and Percentage Constraints: Formulating proportional limits as creates a non-linear fractional expression. Decision variables must be cleared from denominators via cross-multiplication prior to model entry: , yielding .
  • Sign Reversal on Inequality Splitting: When splitting , reversing the second condition requires negating both the coefficient vector and the scalar constant: . Forgetting to negate introduces false boundaries.
  • Implicit Non-Negativity: Real-world quantities (such as tons of paint or pounds of feed) cannot be negative. Omitting allows solvers to generate economically meaningless solutions where unconstrained negative production generates artificial profits or satisfies blending requirements.
1.6 Graphical Solution Method and Geometric Outcomes in 2D

The graphical solution method is a visual, geometric technique used to solve two-variable linear programs (). Because two-dimensional space allows direct plotting on a Cartesian coordinate system, the method translates the algebraic inequalities into geometric boundaries, revealing the structural relationship between the constraints, the gradient of the objective function, and the location of optimal solutions.

1.6.1 The Two-Step Graphical Procedure and Level Line Geometry

Every linear programming problem with two decision variables and is solved graphically in two primary stages:

  1. Delineating the Feasible Solution Space: Each inequality constraint (or ) partitions the plane into two regions separated by the straight boundary line . The set of points satisfying the inequality forms a closed half-plane (or half-space in two dimensions). The feasible solution space (or feasible region) is the intersection of all half-planes defined by the functional constraints together with the non-negativity restrictions and : Because the intersection of any collection of closed convex sets is convex, forms a convex polygonal region whose boundary consists of straight line segments and whose intersections are called corner points or extreme points (vertices).

  2. Sweeping Objective Level Lines: An objective level line (also known as an isocost or isoprofit line) is the locus of all points that yield a fixed objective value : Differentiating implicitly shows that every level line has a fixed slope (for ). Geometrically, all level lines are parallel to each other and strictly orthogonal (perpendicular) to the objective gradient vector: The vector points directly in the direction of the steepest increase of :

    • In a maximization problem, the level line is translated parallel to itself in the direction of (increasing ). The optimal value occurs at the last contact point—the final feasible point the line touches before exiting .
    • In a minimization problem, the level line is translated in the direction opposite to (decreasing ). The optimal value occurs at the first contact point—the point of entry where the line first intersects when sweeping inward toward the origin or the boundary.

1.6.4 Common Pitfalls
  • Sweeping Direction vs. Optimization Sense: A frequent error is sweeping the objective line in the direction of when solving a minimization problem. Moving in the direction of the gradient always increases ; minimization requires translating the level line in the direction of to find the minimum entry contact point.
  • Infeasible Intersection Vertices: Setting pairs of constraint boundary equations to equality generates intersection points in the plane. Not all intersection points are valid vertices of ; many violate one or more of the remaining inequalities or the non-negativity conditions. Only intersections that satisfy all constraints belong to and serve as candidate optima.
  • Overlooking Non-Vertex Optima in Alternative Optima: When multiple optima exist, stating that only the corner points (e.g., points and ) are optimal is incorrect. Every interior point along the line segment joining those vertices is also optimal and yields the exact same objective value.
1.7 The Geometric-Algebraic Bridge: Slack Variables, Basic Solutions, and BFS

The feasible region of a linear program defined by linear inequalities forms a convex polyhedron containing an uncountably infinite continuum of candidate points. The fundamental insight of linear programming is that the optimum of a linear objective over such a region always occurs at an extreme point (or geometric corner point / vertex). Because a polygon or polyhedron has only a finite number of vertices, an infinite search space collapses into a finite combinatorial search. Translating geometric vertices into computational algebra requires the geometric-algebraic bridge.

1.7.1 Augmented Standard Form and Variable Partitioning

Consider a system of linear inequality constraints in original decision variables (, with ). To enable algebraic manipulation, each “” inequality is converted into an exact equality by introducing an auxiliary non-negative variable:

  • Slack variable: For the -th constraint , the slack variable represents the unused resource or slack:
  • Augmented standard equality form: Combining original decision variables and slack variables yields an underdetermined linear system of equations in non-negative variables (, where ):
  • Nonbasic variables: A choice of variables deliberately set to zero. Geometrically, setting a variable to zero forces the solution onto a constraint boundary hyperplane ( corresponds to a coordinate boundary; corresponds to reaching the boundary of the -th structural constraint ).
  • Basic variables: The remaining variables whose values are uniquely determined by solving the square system formed by the columns of corresponding to those variables (termed the basis matrix , provided ).
  • Basic solution: The vector resulting from setting nonbasic variables to zero and solving the linear equations for the basic variables.
  • Combinatorial bound: The maximum number of distinct basic solutions is the number of ways to choose basic variables out of total variables:
  • Basic Feasible Solution (BFS): A basic solution in which all basic variables satisfy the non-negativity condition ( for all ). Every BFS maps bijectively to a geometric vertex (extreme point) of the feasible polytope.
  • Infeasible basic solution: A basic solution where one or more basic variables take strictly negative values. Geometrically, this corresponds to an intersection of constraint boundary lines/planes lying strictly outside the feasible space.

1.7.3 Key Pitfalls
  • Confusing Basic Solutions with Basic Feasible Solutions: Every BFS is a basic solution, but not every basic solution is feasible. An algebraic solution where a basic variable is negative (such as at point ) satisfies the equality equations , but violates non-negativity . It must not be considered as an optimal candidate.
  • Assuming All Boundary Intersections Are Feasible Vertices: Two constraint boundary lines intersecting in always yield an algebraic solution, but that intersection point may violate a third constraint. Only intersections where all other constraints remain satisfied correspond to actual vertices of the feasible region.
  • Assuming Every Variable Partition Yields a Basic Solution: Setting variables to zero yields a basic solution if and only if the columns of the chosen basic variables are linearly independent (). If the columns are linearly dependent, the system has either zero or infinitely many solutions, and no unique basic solution exists for that partition.
1.8 The Simplex Method via Algebraic Dictionaries

The simplex method is an iterative algebraic algorithm designed to solve linear programming problems by traversing adjacent basic feasible solutions along the edges of the feasible polyhedron until reaching an optimal vertex. In its foundational algebraic presentation, the system is manipulated via a sequence of dictionaries.

A dictionary is an equivalent linear system of equations in which the objective variable and a chosen set of basic variables (dependent variables) are expressed explicitly in terms of the remaining nonbasic variables (independent variables):

where is the index set of basic variables, is the index set of nonbasic variables, is the current objective value, and guarantees primal feasibility. The point obtained by setting all nonbasic variables for all yields the associated basic feasible solution (BFS): for , with objective value .

1.8.1 Iteration Mechanics: Entering Variable, Ratio Test, and Pivoting

Every simplex iteration transitions from a current dictionary to an adjacent one of strictly higher (or equal) objective value through four precise steps:

  1. Entering Variable Selection: In a maximization problem, an independent variable () is eligible to enter the basis if its objective coefficient is strictly positive (). Increasing from zero increases . A standard heuristic (Dantzig’s rule) selects the variable with the largest positive coefficient.
  2. The Minimum Ratio Test (Leaving Variable Selection): As the entering variable increases while all other nonbasic variables remain fixed at zero, each basic variable changes according to . To maintain non-negativity (), any row where places an upper bound on : Rows with impose no restriction on increasing . The minimum ratio test identifies the tightest upper bound: The basic variable () achieving this minimum is declared the leaving variable. When reaches , drops to zero.
  3. Pivoting (Algebraic Substitution): Solve the pivot row equation (the leaving variable’s equation) for the entering variable in terms of and the remaining nonbasic variables. Substitute this resulting expression for into all other basic variable equations and into the -row equation. This produces an updated dictionary with new basis and nonbasic set .
  4. Optimality Certificate: If every nonbasic variable in the objective row has a non-positive coefficient ( for all ), no nonbasic variable can be increased without decreasing or maintaining . Because all variables are constrained to be non-negative (), setting nonbasic variables to zero yields the global maximum. The current dictionary proves optimality.

1.8.3 Pitfalls in Dictionary Operations
  • Overlooking Negative or Zero Divisors in the Ratio Test: Only positive coefficients () in the constraint equations restrict the entering variable. A negative coefficient means increasing makes that basic variable larger, never forcing it to violate non-negativity. Including non-positive coefficients in ratio divisions produces invalid leaving variables or division-by-zero errors.
  • Failing to Update the Objective Row: A pivot requires eliminating the entering variable from all equations, including the -row. Leaving the entering variable inside the objective function corrupts the optimality check and masks the true gain in objective value.
  • Selecting Any Nonbasic Variable Regardless of Sign: In a maximization problem, pivoting on a nonbasic variable with a negative objective coefficient () causes the objective value to decrease, moving the algorithm backward away from the optimum.

2. Definitions

  • Optimization problem: A mathematical formulation aimed at finding the values of decision variables that maximize or minimize a given objective function while satisfying all specified constraints.
  • Decision variables: The independent parameters of an optimization model whose numerical values are chosen to optimize the objective criterion.
  • Objective function: The real-valued mathematical expression that quantifies the performance metric, such as profit or cost, to be maximized or minimized.
  • Feasible solution: A vector of decision variable values that satisfies all equality, inequality, and non-negativity constraints of an optimization model simultaneously.
  • Feasible set: The geometric region or solution space formed by the collection of all feasible solutions to an optimization problem.
  • Optimal solution: A feasible solution that yields the most favorable objective function value among all candidate points in the feasible set.
  • Linear program (LP): An optimization problem in which both the objective function and all governing constraints are linear functions of the decision variables.
  • Canonical form: A standardized formulation of a linear program where a linear objective is maximized subject exclusively to less-than-or-equal-to linear inequalities and non-negative variables.
  • Corner point (Extreme point): A boundary vertex of a convex feasible region that cannot be represented as a convex combination of any two distinct points in the set.
  • Slack variable: An auxiliary non-negative variable added to the left-hand side of a less-than-or-equal-to constraint to convert the inequality into an exact equality by absorbing unused capacity.
  • Basic solution: An algebraic solution to a system of linear constraint equations in variables () obtained by setting nonbasic variables to zero and uniquely solving for the remaining basic variables.
  • Basic variables: The subset of dependent variables in an LP system whose values are uniquely determined by solving the constraint equations after fixing nonbasic variables to zero.
  • Nonbasic variables: The subset of independent variables in an LP system whose values are explicitly set to zero to isolate a basic solution.
  • Basic feasible solution (BFS): A basic solution in which all basic variables satisfy non-negativity, corresponding geometrically to a corner point of the feasible region.
  • Simplex dictionary: A rewritten system of linear equations expressing the objective function and the current basic variables explicitly in terms of the nonbasic variables at any simplex iteration.
  • Ratio test: The computational rule in the simplex method that divides current basic values by the positive coefficients of an entering variable to determine the strictest upper bound preventing basic variables from becoming negative.

  • Canonical Form of a Linear Program: ; general compact matrix-vector representation where , , , and .
  • Slack Variable Transformation: with ; converts a inequality constraint into an equivalent equality constraint with a non-negative slack variable .
